title: Transforming and Aggregating DataFrames
summary: Learn to transform and aggregate pandas DataFrames using filtering, grouping, joining, and reshaping so you can summarize raw data into business-ready insights.
objectives: Filter and select DataFrame rows and columns using boolean masks and query expressions
Aggregate data with groupby and named aggregations to compute summary statistics
Combine datasets using merge and join operations with the appropriate join type
Reshape data between wide and long formats using pivot_table, melt, and stack/unstack
Chain transformations into readable pipelines that answer concrete business questions

quiz.q: Which expression correctly filters for rows where country is 'US' AND revenue exceeds 1000?
quiz.why: Each condition must be wrapped in parentheses and combined with & (not the keyword 'and') because of operator precedence and elementwise evaluation.

quiz.q: What does named aggregation like total=('revenue','sum') primarily give you?
options: Conversion from wide to long format
quiz.why: Named aggregation lets you specify the output column name along with the source column and function, producing readable, predictable results.

quiz.q: You merge orders with customers using how='left'. After the merge you have more rows than the original orders table. What is the most likely cause?
options: The join type should have been inner
Duplicate keys in customers caused a many-to-many match
quiz.why: A left join keeps all left rows, but if the right table has duplicate keys each match multiplies rows, increasing the count. Checking counts and using validate= catches this.

quiz.q: Which function converts wide-format data back into long/tidy format?
quiz.why: melt unpivots columns into rows, producing long/tidy data that plotting and modeling tools prefer.

quiz.q: In one sentence, describe the 'split-apply-combine' pattern used by groupby.
quiz.answer: Data is split into groups by key, a function is applied to each group, and the results are combined into one summary table.
quiz.why: This three-step pattern is the conceptual foundation of groupby aggregation in pandas.

quiz.q: Which join type keeps ALL rows from both DataFrames, filling missing matches with NaN?
quiz.why: An outer join returns the union of keys from both tables, inserting NaN where one side has no match.

body_markdown:
## Why Transformation and Aggregation Matter

Raw data rarely answers business questions directly. A data scientist's daily work is reshaping messy tables into clean summaries: *average revenue per region*, *churn rate per cohort*, *top products per month*. Pandas gives you a small set of composable verbs—filter, group, join, reshape—that cover the vast majority of these tasks.

## Filtering and Selecting

Use boolean masks to keep the rows you care about:

```python
high_value = df[df["revenue"] > 1000]
recent_us = df[(df["country"] == "US") & (df["year"] >= 2023)]
```

Combine conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or), `~` (not), and wrap each condition in parentheses. For readability, `df.query("revenue > 1000 and country == 'US'")` is often cleaner. Select columns with `df[["a", "b"]]` or `df.loc[:, ["a", "b"]]`.

## Grouping and Aggregating

`groupby` splits the data into groups, applies a function, and combines the results—the *split-apply-combine* pattern.

```python
summary = (
    df.groupby("region")
      .agg(
          total_revenue=("revenue", "sum"),
          avg_order=("revenue", "mean"),
          orders=("order_id", "count"),
      )
      .reset_index()
)
```

Named aggregation (`new_col=("source_col", "func")`) produces clean, predictable column names. You can group by multiple keys: `df.groupby(["region", "year"])`. Use `.reset_index()` to turn group keys back into regular columns.

## Joining DataFrames

Use `merge` to combine tables on shared keys—similar to SQL joins:

```python
orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
```

Join types:
- **inner**: only matching keys in both tables
- **left**: all rows from the left table, matched where possible
- **right**: all rows from the right table
- **outer**: all rows from both, filling gaps with NaN

Always check row counts before and after a join—unexpected growth usually means duplicate keys causing a many-to-many explosion. Use `validate="one_to_many"` to enforce assumptions.

## Reshaping: Wide vs Long

Long (tidy) format has one observation per row; wide format spreads a variable across columns.

```python
# long -> wide
pivot = df.pivot_table(index="region", columns="year",
                       values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")

# wide -> long
long = pivot.reset_index().melt(id_vars="region",
                                var_name="year", value_name="revenue")
```

`pivot_table` aggregates duplicates automatically; `pivot` does not. Use `melt` to unpivot for plotting or modeling, which generally prefer long/tidy data.

## Putting It Together

A typical pipeline filters, joins reference data, groups, and reshapes—often chained with method calls. Keep steps small, name intermediate results when debugging, and validate row counts at each stage. This workflow turns raw transactional data into the summary tables that drive dashboards and decisions.

slides.title: Transforming and Aggregating DataFrames
slides.sub: From raw tables to business answers
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll learn how to transform and aggregate pandas DataFrames. These are the everyday skills that let a data scientist turn raw, messy data into the clean summaries that answer real business questions.

slides.title: The Core Verbs
bullets: Filter: keep relevant rows and columns
Reshape: switch between wide and long
slides.narration: Almost every data wrangling task is a combination of four verbs: filtering to keep what matters, grouping to summarize, joining to bring tables together, and reshaping to change the layout. Master these and you can handle most of what the job throws at you.

slides.title: Filtering Rows
slides.code:
recent = df[(df['country']=='US') & (df['year']>=2023)]
clean = df.query("revenue > 1000 and country == 'US'")
slides.narration: Filtering uses boolean masks—a condition that returns True or False for each row. Combine conditions with the ampersand for and, pipe for or, and tilde for not, wrapping each in parentheses. The query method is often more readable. Select columns with double brackets.

slides.title: Grouping and Aggregating
bullets: Group by one or many keys
slides.narration: Groupby implements split-apply-combine: split the data into groups, apply a function, and combine results. Named aggregation, where you write new_column equals a tuple of source column and function, gives you predictable column names. Call reset_index to turn group keys back into columns.

slides.title: Joining Tables
bullets: Check row counts before and after
slides.narration: Use merge to combine tables on a shared key, just like SQL. Choose inner for only matches, left to keep everything on the left, right or outer as needed. Always check row counts—if rows multiply unexpectedly, you likely have duplicate keys causing a many-to-many explosion. The validate parameter guards against this.

slides.title: Reshaping: Wide and Long
bullets: pivot_table: long to wide, aggregates dupes
Models and plots prefer long format
slides.code:
pivot = df.pivot_table(index='region', columns='year',
                       values='revenue', aggfunc='sum')
long = pivot.reset_index().melt(id_vars='region')
slides.narration: Long, or tidy, format keeps one observation per row; wide format spreads a variable across columns. Use pivot_table to go long to wide—it aggregates duplicates for you, unlike plain pivot. Use melt to go back to long, which most plotting and modeling tools prefer.

slides.title: Building a Pipeline
bullets: Filter, then join, then group, then reshape
Validate row counts at each step
slides.narration: In practice you chain these verbs into a pipeline: filter to the rows you need, join in reference data, group to summarize, and reshape for output. Method chaining keeps the flow readable, but break it into named steps when debugging, and check your row counts along the way.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Four verbs cover most wrangling tasks
Pick the right join and verify counts
Tidy/long data is your default shape
slides.narration: To summarize: four composable verbs—filter, group, join, reshape—cover the vast majority of data wrangling. Use named aggregation for clean output, choose join types deliberately and verify row counts, and default to tidy long-format data. Practice these on real datasets and they'll become second nature.
